feedback: If a learner writes 0.37 or 370 for 37 ÷ 10, return to the chart and slide each digit exactly one column right; show the point stays put and the digits move, and ask 'ten times smaller than 37 — is that near 3 or near 300?'

If a learner writes 0.4 for 4 ÷ 100, show the 4 landing in hundredths with the tenths column empty; ask what must hold the empty tenths place, and establish that without the 0 the value would be ten times too big.
When a learner reads results by digit string, prompt them to name each digit's place value instead ('what is the 7 worth now?').
activities.intendedInsight: Dividing by 10 (or 100) shifts every digit one (or two) places right and makes it ten (or a hundred) times smaller; a placeholder zero is needed whenever a column between the point and a digit is left empty.
learnerActions: Set up a place-value chart with columns labelled hundreds, tens, ones, then a decimal point, then tenths and hundredths.
Place digit cards for 37 (3 in tens, 7 in ones) and predict what dividing by 10 will do.
Divide by 10 by sliding each digit card one column to the RIGHT: the 3 moves from tens to ones, the 7 moves from ones to tenths, giving 3.7. Notice the decimal point itself does not move.
Read the result back by place value: '3 ones and 7 tenths'.
Now place a single digit card for 4 in the ones column and divide by 100 by sliding it two columns right, so the 4 lands in hundredths.
Notice the tenths column is now empty and write a 0 to hold that place, giving 0.04. Say why, without the 0, you would wrongly read 0.4.

Optionally model the same shrink with another representation — base-ten blocks with exchange (letting a flat be one whole so a rod is a tenth of a flat and a small cube a hundredth), a Gattegno tenths/hundredths chart, or a number line — to see the quantity becoming ten or a hundred times smaller.
activities.title: Slide the digits right on a place-value chart

feedback: If a learner stalls trying to remove a zero from 37, point to the pair 40 ÷ 10 (works) versus 37 ÷ 10 (fails) and rebuild using the digit slide.
If a learner keeps 37 unchanged, ask 'is your answer ten times smaller than 37?' to expose the error.
activities.intendedInsight: 'Remove a zero' only works when there is a trailing zero to remove, and 'move the point' gives the right result only when it is applied carefully but does not explain why it works. Sliding each digit one place right and reading place value always works and shows why.
learnerActions: Work out 40 ÷ 10 and notice that 'take a zero off' happens to give 4.
Now try the same rule on 37 ÷ 10 and show it fails — there is no trailing zero to remove, and leaving 37 unchanged (or writing 370) is wrong.
Redo 37 ÷ 10 on the place-value chart by sliding digits right to get 3.7, and state in your own words why the shortcut only worked for 40.

Test 'move the decimal point' similarly and check it against the chart result. Notice that, done correctly, it agrees with the chart, but it does not show that each digit has become ten times smaller.
activities.title: Confront the 'take a zero off' rule

feedback: If a learner gives £0.4 for £4 ÷ 100, relate it to coins: 4p is four hundredths of a pound, so a 0 must hold the tenths (ten-pence) place.
Have the learner read each answer by place value to confirm the magnitude is sensible.
activities.intendedInsight: Dividing by 10 or 100 means a quantity becomes ten or a hundred times smaller, and the place-value result matches real money and metric amounts.
learnerActions: Work out £4 ÷ 100 and connect it to 4p, writing it as £0.04; check the 4 sits in the hundredths (pence-of-a-pound) place.
Work out 37 cm ÷ 10 and express the result as 3.7 cm, checking which column each digit lands in.
For each context, say which digit moved and what it is now worth.
activities.title: Anchor the shrink in money and measurement

feedback: If 0.4 is chosen for 4 ÷ 100, show on the chart that the 4 belongs in hundredths and the tenths place needs a 0.
If 0.004 is chosen, check how many columns the 4 moved: dividing by 100 moves it two places, not three.
Confirm understanding by asking the learner to name each digit's place value, not just the numeral.
activities.intendedInsight: A correct answer must place every digit in the right column, using a placeholder zero where a column is emptied; the 0.4-versus-0.04 distinction is the sharpest test.
learnerActions: Complete 37 ÷ 10 = ___ and state what each digit is worth.
Choose the correct value of 4 ÷ 100 from 0.4, 0.04, and 0.004, and justify the choice by naming where the 4 lands.
Match each digit in your answers to its place value (ones, tenths, hundredths).
activities.title: Check placeholder and magnitude with targeted questions

feedback: If a learner can label landing places but cannot produce them, return to physically sliding the digits so the movement is performed, not just read.
activities.intendedInsight: A fixed chart names where digits land and supports recall of place-value labels, as a companion to enacting the movement.
learnerActions: Beside the moving chart, keep a labelled still chart and point to where each digit of 37 starts and where it lands after ÷10.
Use it to look up and name the place value of any digit in a result (for example, the hundredths place in 0.04).
activities.title: Static chart as a reference label
